lines.text: A small country between two giants, with a big heart for football, tango and fairness. This is the story of Uruguay.
In 1680 the Portuguese built a town across the river from Buenos Aires: Colonia del Sacramento, whose old streets still stand.
Spain answered in 1724 by founding Montevideo on the great bay. It would become the capital.
Jose Artigas, born in 1764, would lead the people of the Banda Oriental in their fight for freedom, and become the national hero.
In 1825 patriots declared the land free of Brazil, and a new country began to take shape between its two neighbours.
Three years later a treaty made it official: Uruguay was an independent nation.
Jose Batlle y Ordonez, born in 1856, would become the president who built one of the first welfare states in the Americas.
From 1864 Uruguay fought beside Brazil and Argentina against Paraguay, in one of the bloodiest wars South America has known.
In the port districts of Montevideo and Buenos Aires, a new music and dance was born. Tango would soon conquer Paris.
In 1930, a hundred years after its first constitution, Uruguay built the Estadio Centenario for the very first World Cup.
Thirteen teams came, many by ship. In the final, Uruguay beat Argentina, and became the first world champions.
Jose Mujica, born in 1935, would go from guerrilla to prisoner to president, famous as the world's poorest president.
In 1950 Uruguay stunned Brazil at the Maracana in front of a vast crowd, a defeat Brazil still calls the Maracanazo.
Yamandu Orsi, born in 1967, would be elected president in 2025.
But in 1973 the army took power. For twelve years Uruguay lived under dictatorship, until democracy returned in 1985.
And in 1987 Luis Suarez was born, who would become Uruguay's greatest goalscorer.
Small in size but never in spirit, Uruguay still plays above its weight.
